    "proposal/task_brief": "# Growth effects of gene and reaction knockouts in the E. coli core metabolic model\n\n## Objective\n\nYou are given the curated \"textbook\" E. coli core metabolic model (SBML). Using flux balance analysis (FBA), determine how every possible single-gene deletion, single-reaction deletion and pairwise reaction deletion affects the maximal achievable growth (the maximum of the model's biomass objective), plus the growth of a few specific knockouts that illustrate gene-level redundancy (isozymes) for phosphofructokinase.\n\nFor each knockout scenario the quantity of interest is the optimal value of the model's biomass objective after the knockout is applied, together with the status reported by the LP solve (\"optimal\" or \"infeasible\").\n\n## Supplied inputs\n\n- `inputs/e_coli_core.xml` \u2014 the E. coli core metabolic model in SBML format (the model known as \"textbook\" / BiGG `e_coli_core`), including its biomass objective reaction and gene\u2013protein\u2013reaction (GPR) associations. Use the model exactly as supplied; do not modify it, its medium, bounds or objective.\n\n## Knockout semantics\n\n- **Reaction knockout**: the reaction is deleted from any flux-carrying solution \u2014 its flux is constrained to zero in both directions.\n- **Gene knockout**: a reaction is disabled only if its GPR rule evaluates to false with the knocked-out gene(s) removed. If a reaction has an isozyme gene that remains functional (e.g. an OR in the GPR), the reaction still carries flux. A gene whose removal disables no reaction therefore has no growth effect even though the gene is knocked out.\n\n## Required outputs\n\nProduce four CSV files. All use the columns `knockouts,growth,status`:\n\n- `knockouts`: the identifier(s) of the knocked-out entity (gene id or reaction id, exactly as defined in the supplied model), sorted lexicographically and joined with `;` (e.g. `b1723;b3916`, `Biomass_Ecoli_core;LDH_D`). For a knockout of a single entity the label is just that entity's id.\n- `growth`: the optimal objective value of the LP after the knockout, as reported by the solver at full double precision, with no rounding, clamping or sign correction (tiny negative numerical values of magnitude ~1e-14 that arise from solver noise are expected and must be reported as-is). If the knockout makes the problem infeasible, leave this field empty.\n- `status`: the LP solve status string, e.g. `optimal` or `infeasible`.\n\n### 1. `single_gene_deletions.csv`\nOne row for **every gene defined in the supplied model** (including genes whose deletion disables no reaction), reporting the effect of knocking out that gene alone.\n\n### 2. `single_reaction_deletions.csv`\nOne row for **every reaction defined in the supplied model** (this includes boundary/exchange reactions), reporting the effect of knocking out that reaction alone.\n\n### 3. `double_reaction_deletions.csv`\nOne row for **each distinct set of one or two reactions** obtained by pairing every reaction in the model with every reaction in the model and reducing the pair to an unordered set. Concretely: for all ordered pairs (r_i, r_j) over the model's full reaction list, the resulting knockout sets {r_i, r_j}; the i = j cases contribute the single-reaction sets {r_i}. Do not apply gene-level GPR logic here \u2014 both reactions are knocked out directly. Report growth and status for each set.\n\n### 4. `pfk_knockout_optima.csv`\nFour rows, using the same column convention, with an empty `knockouts` field for the no-knockout row:\n\n| knockouts | scenario |\n|---|---|\n| *(empty)* | wild-type model, no knockout |\n| `PFK` | the PFK reaction knocked out |\n| `b1723` | gene b1723 (pfkA) knocked out |\n| `b1723;b3916` | genes b1723 (pfkA) and b3916 (pfkB) knocked out simultaneously |\n\nThese quantify the redundancy narrative: the isozyme pfkB can compensate for a pfkA deletion, but not when both are removed.\n\n## Conventions\n\n- Row order in every file carries no scientific meaning; any row ordering is acceptable.\n- Growth is reported in the model's native biomass-objective units (the raw LP objective value).\n- Use the knockout populations exactly as defined above; do not skip entities that have no reaction associations or no growth effect.\n- Do not round any value (`growth` is written at full double precision).\n\n## Environment and resources\n\n- CPU only (up to 4 cores), 8 GiB RAM, 10 GiB disk, no network access. Your program must complete within 600 seconds.\n- A reference Python environment (cobrapy 0.32.1 with the GLPK solver) can be supplied for convenience, but any software stack that satisfies the definitions above is acceptable; the results, not the tool, are what is compared.\n- Exact acceptance criteria (including numerical tolerances appropriate for LP-solver variation) are finalized separately during validation before the contract takes effect; produce results faithful to the definitions above.",
    "proposal/validation_handoff": "# Validation handoff (private)\n\n## Measured facts (evidence, not ground truth)\n- Reference artifacts on record (same model, default FBA): `single_gene_deletions.csv` (sha256 576e00fe\u2026, 137 data rows + header), `single_reaction_deletions.csv` (e2766a64\u2026, 95 rows), `double_reaction_deletions.csv` (9169de53\u2026, 4560 rows). Columns observed: `knockouts,growth,status`; empty `growth` fields paired with status `infeasible` (2 / 2 / 352 rows respectively); status vocabulary observed: {optimal, infeasible} only (structural observation, not a guarantee).\n- Row counts are model properties: 137 genes, 95 reactions, 95 + C(95,2) = 4560 reaction sets (singletons from self-pairs are part of the double-deletion population per `deletion.py` line 208).\n- Reference stdout (trial log, private): complete 0.874; PFK KO 0.704; b1723 KO 0.874; b1723+b3916 KO 0.704 \u2014 consistent with projections of tables 1/2 (PFK and b1723 rows) and defines the wild-type and double-gene values for table 4. stdout is cross-evidence, not an independent rerun.\n- Replay observations (two fresh runs): identical headers, stable row counts, but differing byte hashes and differing row-multiset fingerprints. Explanation: (a) row order comes from Python set-of-frozensets iteration and is run-dependent \u2014 order is a scientific non-invariance target, comparisons must be order-free; (b) low-order float digits vary between solves (0.9166474637510491 vs 0.9166474637510509 etc.) \u2014 LP degeneracy/alternate optima; requires calibrated numeric tolerance, uncalibrated here. Tiny negative growth values occur (single tables min \u2248 -3.74e-15, double min \u2248 -6.79e-14) and must not be clamped if source fidelity is to be preserved.\n\n## Input derivation (to be materialized by construction)\n- Task input `inputs/e_coli_core.xml` does not yet exist as an artifact. Intended derivation: the \"textbook\" model bundled with the reference environment \u2014 cobra 0.32.1 package data `cobra/data/textbook.xml.gz` (SBML, BiGG id `e_coli_core`), i.e. exactly what `load_model(\"textbook\")` returns in cobra 0.32.1. Materialize the decompressed SBML at the stated task-relative path, pin its identity (size/sha256), and verify that the solver-loaded model yields the documented 137 genes / 95 reactions / 4465 distinct reaction pairs. This is a proposed derived input, not yet built or validated.\n- No other inputs. iJO1366 is not part of the task (only used by the excluded timing benchmark).\n\n## Endpoint lineage\n- Table 1 \u2190 `single_gene_deletion(cobra_model)` (call-50). Table 2 \u2190 `single_reaction_deletion(cobra_model)` (call-96). Table 3 \u2190 `double_reaction_deletion(cobra_model)` (call-97). Tables 1\u20133 have existing reference CSVs produced by the reference script's append-only export (frozenset labels \u2192 \";\".join(sorted(ids)), NaN growth \u2192 empty CSV field via pandas defaults).\n- Table 4 (`pfk_knockout_optima.csv`) has **no existing reference artifact**. Construction must generate it by faithful recomputation of the original with-block calls (calls 32\u201344) on the same unmodified model: wild-type `optimize()`; PFK reaction knockout then optimize; b1723 knockout then optimize; b1723+b3916 both knocked out then optimize. No reference values for this file have been measured beyond the printed stdout optima; it needs independent generation and validation. `knockouts` label for the wild-type row is an empty field under this task's stated convention (the source has no label for it; this is a new, explicitly documented representation choice).\n- Method facts (verified in cobra 0.32.1 source, cited in review): default `method=\"fba\"`; growth = `slim_optimize()` objective value; `SolverError` \u2192 NaN + solver status; GPR-based gene knockout with isozyme tolerance; reaction knockout = bounds (0,0) both directions; double-reaction population includes singletons from {r, r} self-pairs; row order from set iteration is nondeterministic and scientifically meaningless.\n\n## Exclusions (source-backed)\n- iJO1366 double-gene runs and all timing prints (calls 26\u201383 timing parts): nondeterministic multiprocessing benchmark; narrative frames them only as such.\n- Subset demo calls 54, 58, 87\u201388: covered by projections of tables 1\u20133 (same populations, prefix/positional slices, identical operations).\n- `double_gene_deletion(genes[-5:]).round(4)` (calls 64\u201365): mechanics demonstration, value discarded (bare expression; not printed in script run); `.round(4)` is display formatting. Flagged as a judgment call \u2014 if validation deems this an eligible endpoint, it can only be recovered by faithful recomputation over the model's gene order (positional slice `genes[-5:]`); no reference exists.\n- `.knockout[]` prints (calls 99\u2013100, 108\u2013109): projections of tables 2/3 rows.\n\n## Unresolved construction/validation questions\n1. Materialization and identity pinning of `inputs/e_coli_core.xml` (above), and confirmation that a solver rebuild from this file reproduces the declared gene/reaction populations.\n2. Generation and independent validation of `pfk_knockout_optima.csv` (no reference artifact yet).\n3. Comparison design (validation-owned): order-free row comparison; numerical tolerance for `growth` (unrounded doubles, LP degeneracy and cross-solver variation; tiny negatives must be accommodated rather than clamped); status-string comparison; treatment of the four table-4 rows (wild-type empty `knockouts` label).\n4. Whether any status other than {optimal, infeasible} can occur for this model and knockouts (only the two were observed structurally).\n5. Timing feasibility: full double-reaction sweep completed in ~12 s in the reference sandbox (600 s limit); solver-side portability to other LP solvers untested.\n\nTolerances, comparator code and pass/fail predictions are deliberately left to the validation stage; nothing here asserts equivalence of alternative stacks beyond the astronomical-unit conventions fixed above.",

    "trial/reference.py": "# ---\n# jupyter:\n#   jupytext:\n#     text_representation:\n#       extension: .py\n#       format_name: nomarker\n#       format_version: '1.0'\n#       jupytext_version: 1.19.6\n#   kernelspec:\n#     display_name: Python 3 (ipykernel)\n#     language: python\n#     name: python3\n# ---\n\n# # Simulating Deletions\n\nimport pandas\nfrom time import time\n\nfrom cobra.io import load_model\nfrom cobra.flux_analysis import (\n    single_gene_deletion, single_reaction_deletion, double_gene_deletion,\n    double_reaction_deletion)\n\ncobra_model = load_model(\"textbook\")\necoli_model = load_model(\"iJO1366\")\n\n# ## Knocking out single genes and reactions\n\n# A commonly asked question when analyzing metabolic models is what will happen if a certain reaction was not allowed to have any flux at all. This can tested using cobrapy by\n\nprint('complete model: ', cobra_model.optimize())\nwith cobra_model:\n    cobra_model.reactions.PFK.knock_out()\n    print('pfk knocked out: ', cobra_model.optimize())\n\n# For evaluating genetic manipulation strategies, it is more interesting to examine what happens if given genes are knocked out as doing so can affect no reactions in case of redundancy, or more reactions if gene when is participating in more than one reaction.\n\nprint('complete model: ', cobra_model.optimize())\nwith cobra_model:\n    cobra_model.genes.b1723.knock_out()\n    print('pfkA knocked out: ', cobra_model.optimize())\n    cobra_model.genes.b3916.knock_out()\n    print('pfkB knocked out: ', cobra_model.optimize())\n\n# ## Single Deletions\n\n# Perform all single gene deletions on a model\n\ndeletion_results = single_gene_deletion(cobra_model)\n\n# These can also be done for only a subset of genes\n\nsingle_gene_deletion(cobra_model, cobra_model.genes[:20])\n\n# This can also be done for reactions\n\nsingle_reaction_deletion(cobra_model, cobra_model.reactions[:20])\n\n# ## Double Deletions\n\n# Double deletions run in a similar way.\n\ndouble_gene_deletion(\n    cobra_model, cobra_model.genes[-5:]).round(4)\n\n# By default, the double deletion function will automatically use multiprocessing, splitting the task over up to 4 cores if they are available. The number of cores can be manually specified as well. Setting use of a single core will disable use of the multiprocessing library, which often aids debugging.\n\nstart = time()  # start timer()\ndouble_gene_deletion(\n    ecoli_model, ecoli_model.genes[:25], processes=2)\nt1 = time() - start\nprint(\"Double gene deletions for 200 genes completed in \"\n      \"%.2f sec with 2 cores\" % t1)\n\nstart = time()  # start timer()\ndouble_gene_deletion(\n    ecoli_model, ecoli_model.genes[:25], processes=1)\nt2 = time() - start\nprint(\"Double gene deletions for 200 genes completed in \"\n      \"%.2f sec with 1 core\" % t2)\n\nprint(\"Speedup of %.2fx\" % (t2 / t1))\n\n# Double deletions can also be run for reactions.\n\ndouble_reaction_deletion(\n    cobra_model, cobra_model.reactions[2:7]).round(4)\n\n# ## Accessing individual deletion results\n#\n# Note that the indices for deletions are python [set](https://docs.python.org/3.8/library/stdtypes.html#set-types-set-frozenset) objects. This is the appropriate type since the order of deletions does not matter. Deleting reaction 1 and reaction 2 will have the same effect as deleting reaction 2 and reaction 1. \n#\n# To make it easier to access results all DataFrames returned by COBRAPpy deletion functions have a `knockout` indexer that makes that a bit simpler. Each entry in the indexer is treated as a single deletion entry. So you need to pass sets for double deletions.\n\nsingle = single_reaction_deletion(cobra_model)\ndouble = double_reaction_deletion(cobra_model)\n\nprint(single.knockout[\"ATPM\"])\nprint(double.knockout[{\"ATPM\", \"TKT1\"}])\n\n# This can be used to get several deletions at once and will also work for Reaction or Gene objects (depending on what you deleted) directly.\n\natpm = cobra_model.reactions.ATPM\ntkt1 = cobra_model.reactions.TKT1\npfk = cobra_model.reactions.PFK\n\nprint(single.knockout[atpm, tkt1, pfk])\nprint(double.knockout[{atpm, tkt1}, {atpm, pfk}, {atpm}])\n\n\n\n\n\nimport os as _export_os\nimport pandas as _export_pd\n\n_export_dir = \"/work/outputs\"\n_export_os.makedirs(_export_dir, exist_ok=True)\n\n\ndef _format_knockout_ids(knockout_ids):\n    if isinstance(knockout_ids, (set, frozenset, list, tuple)):\n        return \";\".join(sorted(str(identifier) for identifier in knockout_ids))\n    return str(knockout_ids)\n\n\ndef _write_deletion_results(frame, filename):\n    export_frame = frame.copy()\n    if \"ids\" in export_frame.columns:\n        labels = [\n            _format_knockout_ids(value)\n            for value in export_frame[\"ids\"].tolist()\n        ]\n        export_frame = export_frame.drop(columns=\"ids\")\n    else:\n        labels = [\n            _format_knockout_ids(value)\n            for value in export_frame.index.tolist()\n        ]\n    export_frame.index = _export_pd.Index(labels, name=\"knockouts\")\n    export_frame.to_csv(_export_os.path.join(_export_dir, filename))\n\n\n_write_deletion_results(deletion_results, \"single_gene_deletions.csv\")\n_write_deletion_results(single, \"single_reaction_deletions.csv\")\n_write_deletion_results(double, \"double_reaction_deletions.csv\")",

08 · Construct reference, inputs and oracle

Prompt

Actual system prompt

autonomous-runs/226/explorer-evidence/materialization-raw/materialize/system-prompt.md

Materialize a proposed scientific task from existing evidence

You are a GLM worker building supplied task inputs and a reference solution. Treat the earlier public draft as a proposal to check against the source and actual inputs. Preserve the scientific question and computations, while correcting unsupported explanatory claims. Avoid unnecessary textbook definitions; verify consequential logical conditions and quantifiers instead of paraphrasing encoded input rules from memory. Keep the public task concise and scientifically accurate. The original source and policy define the scientific scope; the latest specification is a proposal to check against them. The preparation inventory describes what could be saved without editing the source, not which scientific branches belong in the task. Preserve every eligible source endpoint across all branches in one task. An endpoint omitted by a proposal or unavailable in the preparation exports still requires faithful recovery when policy permits, or a concrete blocker. Preparatory intermediates need not become requested outputs. Do not copy the original function-by-function recipe into the public question.

The proposed question cannot redefine source scope to exclude another scientific branch. A distinct quantitative comparison of biological observations can be an endpoint even when introductory, scalar or unnamed. "A different scientific question" is not an exclusion reason; establish a solely mechanical or diagnostic role from source evidence before excluding it as a teaching example.

Submit a complete initial candidate from the supplied source, proposal and recorded observations before using the shell. The controller enforces this ordering: shell commands do not run until a candidate has undergone controlled execution. Use the already executed reference packages and computation for the initial oracle. After execution, tool access is available to inspect the final environment and diagnose a demonstrated runtime failure. If the supplied evidence cannot support a candidate, return a concrete blocked disposition instead of inventing missing scientific facts. Successful construction hands off to independent scientific validation; it does not require you to establish numerical equivalence first.

After successful controlled execution, the controller returns identities for the actual final input/reference/oracle inventory and an installed-asset catalog. The feedback identifies the complete catalog's read-only inspection path, which is accessible to your authoring shell and hidden from the isolated oracle. This includes recovered endpoints; setup's earlier answer-file review does not cover outputs that were not yet selected or recovered. Inspect the actual candidate files and their relationship to the final requested results using the shell. Candidate names, matching numbers or differing bytes alone do not prove that a file is an answer or is unused. An unused file may expose a partial answer in text, code or another representation even without byte identity.

The same feedback also supplies advisory numeric matches between actual installed Python source and the final executed CSV/TSV outputs. Read the complete report at installed_asset_value_hints, including its candidate and reference coverage. Inspect each finding's source, input and scientific quantity before assessing it. An unrelated match is not an answer; the discovery distance is not a grading tolerance. Integers, strings, comments, other formats and nonpriority files remain gaps, and no match does not establish a clean environment. These are private authoring observations, never solver inputs. Use them in the existing environment assessment while you can declare justified unused-file removals; they add no scientific computation or repair allowance. A changed candidate or environment requires fresh controlled execution and new bound observations.

On the initial submission leave environment_review null. After observing the executed inventory, use revise_artifact with {"patch": {"environment_review": ...}} to supply only that field when the scientific candidate is unchanged, or submit a complete replacement. The review must contain the exact returned artifact_inventory_sha256 and asset_catalog_sha256, an evidence-backed assessment, and additional_exclusions (possibly empty). Each new exclusion needs the observed installed distribution, distribution-relative path, exact sha256, and a reason establishing both requested-answer exposure and unused status. Do not remove required data, runtime code or notices. Never delete files through the shell or change scientific methods, inputs or endpoints to hide an answer. Report a blocker if a necessary asset gives away the requested result.

The controller applies only your exact declarations and repeats controlled derivation/oracle execution after a change. Inspect its new observations and resubmit an assessment bound to that final inventory/catalog; retain all earlier additional declarations. No-change assessments reuse the already executed candidate. These steps use the existing construction worker, time and resources. Independent grading/review and native qualification still follow; your assessment does not supply a reward or establish successful isolation by itself.

This is construction, not independent scientific validation; a later blind worker performs that check. Prefer adapting the already executed reference implementation. When prior_worker_draft is supplied, reuse its supported code and repair the remaining gaps from source evidence and inspected inputs. Prior execution does not prove its public contract complete. Submit a complete candidate including unchanged fields, rather than rebuilding a separate implementation without a concrete need.

You receive the source, export evidence, replay observations, and the proposed public task together with its private scientific review. draft_ready means a proposal ready for construction, not an approved or validated scientific contract. Read the review before investigating; preserve its established facts and unresolved questions instead of rediscovering them. Notes about later validation are context, not a request to implement that validation here.

Check the proposal against the supplied input observations. Do not assert an input precondition that has not been measured or retain a known unsupported convention solely because the proposal stated it. You may clarify unsupported incidental conventions without changing the scientific target; explain the evidence and each clarification in the rationale. A substantive methodological change requires a blocker, not a silent repair. Leave unresolved numerical equivalence to the comparison stage; do not attempt repeated full independent implementations before submitting a candidate. Grader design and independent-implementation plans belong to later workers. Verify that public units and scales describe the produced values, including any reader/library conversions; source table headings alone are insufficient. An accurate output-column label or explicit reversible unit conversion is a representation change only when it preserves the same source-computed quantity. Document its exact mapping, retain original reference bytes and produce the derived representation separately. Do not change scientific methods, reinterpret the physical quantity, or retain a known false unit merely to match a source label. The shell runs in a locked Python environment, offline. /work/reference contains read-only original terminal artifacts. original_inputs identifies read-only original input files and their recorded identities. Work under /work/author. Preserve recorded reference artifacts unchanged. If an existing export already meets a requested output schema, copy its bytes even when the destination filename changes; do not read and serialize it again without a concrete need. Inspect the actual exported schema and values before projecting or converting them, rather than assuming they still have their in-memory source types. Treat serialized identifiers as opaque values unless the source explicitly defines their structure; a string is not a collection of its component entities. Any necessary projection or conversion must preserve entity correspondence, row multiplicity, missingness and numeric precision, with its mapping documented in the rationale. Verify that mapping against the recorded artifact; a successful program and matching row counts alone do not establish identity preservation. When policy permits, recover a required scientific endpoint absent from those exports by rerunning its original source computation with unchanged methods, arguments, original inputs and required input state. Keep this recovery separate from the recorded reference, document source locations and state/dependency lineage, and let controlled execution and subsequent independent validation check it. An unnamed or overwritten result alone is not permission to drop a scientific branch. Do not guess missing state, repair source defects, change methods or inputs, add a new analysis, or reconstruct plotting internals. Block if faithful recovery cannot be established. Avoid unrelated upstream work.

Return a complete structured artifact:

  • instruction: standalone solver question with scientific methods, inputs under inputs/, outputs under outputs/, identifiers, schemas and resource limits. No private paths, measured answer values or exhaustive API recipe. Grading tolerances remain pending validation; do not invent them. Keep pipeline status and pending-validation notes in the private rationale, not the solver question. The controller will append the validated acceptance rules before solving.
  • input_paths, output_paths: relative files inside the respective directories.
  • derive_code: Python CLI accepting --source-inputs PATH (JSON manifest of original absolute paths), --reference-dir PATH (original terminal artifacts), and --destination PATH. Create only destination/inputs/ and destination/reference/. Copy original task data byte-for-byte where required, derive proposed supplied metadata by selecting existing fields, and project selected answer fields from existing reference exports. Where policy permits source-faithful recovery, also save recovered endpoints under the new destination with explicit provenance; retain the original reference untouched. No invented answer values, new analysis or changed scientific methods/inputs. Document the source computation, required state and artifact lineage in the rationale.
  • oracle_code: Python CLI accepting --input-dir PATH and --output-dir PATH. Solve the public task using only those supplied inputs. It will run under a separate user without access to reference answers or your working directory. Never embed measured answers, access the original reference, or depend on a hidden cache/author artifact. Use the installed environment; no internet.
  • rationale: private explanation of scope, scientific fidelity, input derivation, possible leakage, output projections and remaining comparison questions. Account for each eligible source endpoint: identify its source computation and corresponding requested output, including any source-faithful recovery. Explain scientific exclusions separately from limits of the preparation export inventory.
  • operation_coverage: account for every ID in the controller's source_operations inventory exactly once; group IDs when their roles and explanation agree. These are syntactic call sites, not an executed DAG or preselected endpoints. Use result for calls producing requested scientific outputs and name their artifact_paths; use supplied_input for an explicitly supplied intermediate and name its input files. Classify other calls as support, presentation, diagnostic or not_executed, with source-backed reasons and empty paths. Use redundant only for a result genuinely obtainable from a retained result or supplied input; give its counterpart_id, empty paths and the projection argument (same operation, entities, input state and parameters). Otherwise counterpart_id is null. The controller rejects absent IDs, missing output provenance, cycles and counterparts with different literal call targets. Matching call targets alone do not establish redundancy: differing arguments, state or populations still need scientific assessment. An unnamed or subset result without a retained counterpart cannot be dismissed as an API example. Do not use support or diagnostic to hide an independent scientific branch. The ledger is private evidence for independent review, not proof of coverage.

Validate cell/entity alignment explicitly. Prefer original stable identifiers or explicit composite keys for supplied metadata; avoid making the solver reconstruct an incidental package-specific naming convention when a transparent key can be supplied without changing the science. Supplied intermediate results are reference-derived inputs, not biological ground truth. Retain sufficient identity information without exposing downstream answers. Check claimed input formats and headers against the actual staged files. Inspect the actual input keys and output grain, rather than assuming one source row is one scientific entity. When parsing drops records, distinguish verified metadata and scientifically justified selection from unsupported data loss. Never describe a real observation as a header simply because the reference skips it. Report a source-fidelity blocker when the stated population and actual parsing conflict; do not change the source, input bytes or public population merely to reproduce that defect. If the necessary file observations are unavailable, state the evidence gap instead of inventing them. When several source rows share an entity key, check whether their annotations agree. State the intended multiplicity and any rule for selecting or combining conflicting annotations in the public question, supported by the source analysis. Do not leave these as hidden oracle conventions or choose a rule merely to match saved answers; report a blocker if the source and requested task cannot support an explicit rule. Keep the task scientifically substantial. The oracle may use reference packages; the public task does not require those APIs. Do not silently change the requested scientific quantities merely to fit the saved answers. Report a blocker for a genuine incompatibility.

Submit a minimal complete candidate promptly. The controller executes derivation, verifies exact declared inventories and unchanged original input hashes, then runs the oracle from a clean directory for the supplied reference time limit. It returns runtime/schema failures so you can repair your programs. Successful execution alone does not validate numerical equivalence: a separate comparison stage checks the oracle outputs against the projected reference and tests alternatives/errors. Do not spend this stage constructing a grader, a separate clean-room implementation, or a broad mutation suite. Prefer the simplest faithful oracle, normally using the reference packages already installed: adapt the source computation to the proposed scope and supplied inputs. Do not reimplement those packages from statistical primitives in this stage. A fresh worker will independently implement the public question during comparison validation; do not duplicate that stage here. Still report an actual conflict between the public definition and the reference.

Use disposition: ready or blocked; explain blockers in rationale. Tools are shell, submit_artifact and revise_artifact. Do not claim tests you did not run.

Shell execution

Keep diagnostics concise: print aggregate checks and representative examples. Save complete listings to scratch files and inspect selected sections instead of streaming all rows, arrays or mismatches into the conversation.

Where the public question frees row order or textual number formatting, do not reverse-engineer those incidental choices just to match file bytes. A later stage compares scientific content under the validated public contract.

Run commands in the foreground. Each shell call terminates its remaining child processes when it returns; background/nohup work cannot continue between calls. For longer computations, explicitly set timeout_sec up to the supplied reference_seconds limit (the shell default is 120 seconds). Save useful results to files before returning, then inspect them in later calls.

    "candidate/pyproject.toml": "[project]\nname = \"cobrapy-deletions-setup\"\nversion = \"0.1.0\"\nrequires-python = \">=3.13\"\ndependencies = [\n  \"cobra==0.32.1\",\n]\n",
    "inputs/exports.py": "import os as _export_os\nimport pandas as _export_pd\n\n_export_dir = \"/work/outputs\"\n_export_os.makedirs(_export_dir, exist_ok=True)\n\n\ndef _format_knockout_ids(knockout_ids):\n    if isinstance(knockout_ids, (set, frozenset, list, tuple)):\n        return \";\".join(sorted(str(identifier) for identifier in knockout_ids))\n    return str(knockout_ids)\n\n\ndef _write_deletion_results(frame, filename):\n    export_frame = frame.copy()\n    if \"ids\" in export_frame.columns:\n        labels = [\n            _format_knockout_ids(value)\n            for value in export_frame[\"ids\"].tolist()\n        ]\n        export_frame = export_frame.drop(columns=\"ids\")\n    else:\n        labels = [\n            _format_knockout_ids(value)\n            for value in export_frame.index.tolist()\n        ]\n    export_frame.index = _export_pd.Index(labels, name=\"knockouts\")\n    export_frame.to_csv(_export_os.path.join(_export_dir, filename))\n\n\n_write_deletion_results(deletion_results, \"single_gene_deletions.csv\")\n_write_deletion_results(single, \"single_reaction_deletions.csv\")\n_write_deletion_results(double, \"double_reaction_deletions.csv\")",
    "inputs/original.py": "# ---\n# jupyter:\n#   jupytext:\n#     text_representation:\n#       extension: .py\n#       format_name: nomarker\n#       format_version: '1.0'\n#       jupytext_version: 1.19.6\n#   kernelspec:\n#     display_name: Python 3 (ipykernel)\n#     language: python\n#     name: python3\n# ---\n\n# # Simulating Deletions\n\nimport pandas\nfrom time import time\n\nfrom cobra.io import load_model\nfrom cobra.flux_analysis import (\n    single_gene_deletion, single_reaction_deletion, double_gene_deletion,\n    double_reaction_deletion)\n\ncobra_model = load_model(\"textbook\")\necoli_model = load_model(\"iJO1366\")\n\n# ## Knocking out single genes and reactions\n\n# A commonly asked question when analyzing metabolic models is what will happen if a certain reaction was not allowed to have any flux at all. This can tested using cobrapy by\n\nprint('complete model: ', cobra_model.optimize())\nwith cobra_model:\n    cobra_model.reactions.PFK.knock_out()\n    print('pfk knocked out: ', cobra_model.optimize())\n\n# For evaluating genetic manipulation strategies, it is more interesting to examine what happens if given genes are knocked out as doing so can affect no reactions in case of redundancy, or more reactions if gene when is participating in more than one reaction.\n\nprint('complete model: ', cobra_model.optimize())\nwith cobra_model:\n    cobra_model.genes.b1723.knock_out()\n    print('pfkA knocked out: ', cobra_model.optimize())\n    cobra_model.genes.b3916.knock_out()\n    print('pfkB knocked out: ', cobra_model.optimize())\n\n# ## Single Deletions\n\n# Perform all single gene deletions on a model\n\ndeletion_results = single_gene_deletion(cobra_model)\n\n# These can also be done for only a subset of genes\n\nsingle_gene_deletion(cobra_model, cobra_model.genes[:20])\n\n# This can also be done for reactions\n\nsingle_reaction_deletion(cobra_model, cobra_model.reactions[:20])\n\n# ## Double Deletions\n\n# Double deletions run in a similar way.\n\ndouble_gene_deletion(\n    cobra_model, cobra_model.genes[-5:]).round(4)\n\n# By default, the double deletion function will automatically use multiprocessing, splitting the task over up to 4 cores if they are available. The number of cores can be manually specified as well. Setting use of a single core will disable use of the multiprocessing library, which often aids debugging.\n\nstart = time()  # start timer()\ndouble_gene_deletion(\n    ecoli_model, ecoli_model.genes[:25], processes=2)\nt1 = time() - start\nprint(\"Double gene deletions for 200 genes completed in \"\n      \"%.2f sec with 2 cores\" % t1)\n\nstart = time()  # start timer()\ndouble_gene_deletion(\n    ecoli_model, ecoli_model.genes[:25], processes=1)\nt2 = time() - start\nprint(\"Double gene deletions for 200 genes completed in \"\n      \"%.2f sec with 1 core\" % t2)\n\nprint(\"Speedup of %.2fx\" % (t2 / t1))\n\n# Double deletions can also be run for reactions.\n\ndouble_reaction_deletion(\n    cobra_model, cobra_model.reactions[2:7]).round(4)\n\n# ## Accessing individual deletion results\n#\n# Note that the indices for deletions are python [set](https://docs.python.org/3.8/library/stdtypes.html#set-types-set-frozenset) objects. This is the appropriate type since the order of deletions does not matter. Deleting reaction 1 and reaction 2 will have the same effect as deleting reaction 2 and reaction 1. \n#\n# To make it easier to access results all DataFrames returned by COBRAPpy deletion functions have a `knockout` indexer that makes that a bit simpler. Each entry in the indexer is treated as a single deletion entry. So you need to pass sets for double deletions.\n\nsingle = single_reaction_deletion(cobra_model)\ndouble = double_reaction_deletion(cobra_model)\n\nprint(single.knockout[\"ATPM\"])\nprint(double.knockout[{\"ATPM\", \"TKT1\"}])\n\n# This can be used to get several deletions at once and will also work for Reaction or Gene objects (depending on what you deleted) directly.\n\natpm = cobra_model.reactions.ATPM\ntkt1 = cobra_model.reactions.TKT1\npfk = cobra_model.reactions.PFK\n\nprint(single.knockout[atpm, tkt1, pfk])\nprint(double.knockout[{atpm, tkt1}, {atpm, pfk}, {atpm}])\n\n\n\n",
    "inputs/plan.json": "{\n  \"artifacts\": [\n    {\n      \"description\": \"Growth rates for all single gene knockouts of the complete textbook model.\",\n      \"path\": \"single_gene_deletions.csv\",\n      \"source_evidence\": \"Produced by `deletion_results = single_gene_deletion(cobra_model)` under '## Single Deletions' with the narrative 'Perform all single gene deletions on a model'. These are display-only illustrations of the same functions on smaller subsets; the complete-model results covering them are exported above.\",\n    \"Endpoint unavailable for append-only export (printed demonstration values): the knocked-out model growth rates shown by `print('pfk knocked out: ', cobra_model.optimize())` and the pfkA/pfkB prints inside `with cobra_model:` blocks. Recovery would need to record the optimize() return values within those original context blocks in the source script.\"\n  ],\n  \"explanation\": \"The notebook's terminal scientific products are the systematic in-silico deletion results for the complete textbook model: all single gene deletions (`deletion_results`), all single reaction deletions (`single`), and all double reaction deletions (`double`), which the narrative interprets via growth values and the `knockout` indexer.   "specification": {
    "review": "# Private review\n\n## Scope and endpoint selection\nThe notebook's terminal scientific products are systematic in-silico FBA deletion analyses of the complete E. coli core (\"textbook\") model, plus the interpreted single-knockout demonstrations in the first section. Selected endpoints (all on the unmodified textbook model, default FBA method):\n\n1. `single_gene_deletions.csv` \u2190 `deletion_results = single_gene_deletion(cobra_model)` (call-50).\n2. `single_reaction_deletions.csv` \u2190 `single = single_reaction_deletion(cobra_model)` (call-96).\n3. `double_reaction_deletions.csv` \u2190 `double = double_reaction_deletion(cobra_model)` (call-97).\n4. `pfk_knockout_optima.csv` \u2190 the printed context-block optima (calls 32\u201344): wild-type, PFK reaction knockout, b1723 knockout, b1723+b3916 simultaneous knockout. The plan.json marked these endpoint-unavailable for append-only export; per the endpoint-recovery policy these are recovered as an assigned task output computed from the same supplied model by the same methods (the with-blocks restore the model, so no hidden state is involved). PFK- and b1723-row values are projections of tables 2 and 1 respectively; the wild-type optimum and the b1723+b3916 double-gene combination are not subsumed by any export, so they must be kept.\n\n## Source-operation coverage ledger\n- call-25 `load_model(\"textbook\")` \u2014 model supplied as task input (see handoff).\n- calls 26, 69, 70, 72\u201380, 76, 77 (`iJO1366` runs, `time()`, speedup print) \u2014 excluded as nondeterministic multiprocessing timing benchmark; narrative frames them solely as such (\"Speedup of %.2fx\"). Note the print text \"200 genes\" contradicts the 25-gene slice; text bug in the notebook, diagnostic either way.\n- calls 54 (`genes[:20]`), 58 (`reactions[:20]`) \u2014 subtree demonstrations; subsumed by projections of tables 1/2 (same populations restricted to prefixes; narrative: \"These can also be done for only a subset\").\n- calls 64\u201365 (`double_gene_deletion(genes[-5:]).round(4)`) \u2014 mechanics demonstration of the double-deletion API on a positional 5-gene slice, value discarded (not stored, and not even printed in the script run \u2014 bare expression, absent from the reference log), `.round(4)` is display formatting. Excluded as teaching mechanics; the narrative does not interpret its results. Residual judgment call noted for validation; recovery by faithful recomputation would be possible if reviewers disagree.\n- calls 87\u201388 (`reactions[2:7]`) \u2014 subsumed by projection of table 3.\n- calls 99\u2013100, 108\u2013109 (`.knockout` indexer prints) \u2014 reads of rows of tables 2/3; subsumed by stated projections.\n- calls 32\u201344 \u2014 recovered as table 4 above.\n\n## Method facts verified in pinned code (cobra/0.32.1 wheels)\n- `deletion.py` line 208: population `= {frozenset(comb) for comb in product(*element_lists)}`; both entity lists default to the full model reaction/gene list, so the double-reaction population contains each set {r_i, r_j} over all ordered pairs (r, r) \u2192 singletons included). Observed: 95 + C(95,2) = 4560 rows; single tables 137 and 95 rows (structural audit; private cross-check).\n- Row construction `(set(ids), growth, status)`, growth from `slim_optimize()` under default `method=\"fba\"`; `SolverError` \u2192 NaN growth + solver status (observed statuses in audit: \"optimal\", \"infeasible\" only).\n- `Gene.knock_out` (core/gene.py 240\u2013251): Functional\u2192False, zeroes bounds of associated reactions left non-functional per GPR. `Reaction.knock_out`: bounds (0,0), both directions.\n- `args` is a set of frozensets \u21d2 row emission order is set-iteration order, run-dependent. Scientific invariance: order is meaningless.\n\n## Observed fidelity / replay\nReference execution (exit 0, ~12 s, GPUless, offline-capable \u2014 models bundle in cobra package data per outcome.json) produced the three CSVs with columns knockouts/growth/status, hashed in trial/result.json and output-audit.json. Replay runs show identical headers and stable row counts but differing byte hashes and differing row-multiset fingerprints \u2014 explained by run-dependent row order (set iteration) and low-order float digit variation between solves (multiple alternating optima / LP degeneracy; e.g. 0.9166474637510491 vs ...509). Tiny negative growth values present (single tables min \u2248 -3.7e-15, double \u2248 -6.8e-14) and retained unrounded in the reference \u2014 no clamping. mirroring the defined semantics:\n    # wild type, PFK reaction knockout, pfkA gene knockout, and the\n    # simultaneous pfkA + pfkB double gene knockout (sequential knockouts of\n    # both genes on the same model within one context).\n    rows = []\n    solution = model.optimize()\n    rows.append((\"\", _format_growth(solution.objective_value), solution.status))\n    with model:\n        model.reactions.PFK.knock_out()\n        solution = model.optimize()\n        rows.append((\"PFK\", _format_growth(solution.objective_value), solution.status))\n    with model:\n        model.genes.b1723.knock_out()\n        solution = model.optimize()\n        rows.append((\"b1723\", _format_growth(solution.objective_value), solution.status))\n        model.genes.b3916.knock_out()\n        solution = model.optimize()\n        rows.append(\n            (\"b1723;b3916\", _format_growth(solution.objective_value), solution.status)\n        )\n    _write_csv(os.path.join(args.output_dir, \"pfk_knockout_optima.csv\"), header, rows)\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    main()\n",

  "rationale": "SCOPE. The source notebook's terminal scientific products are the complete-model FBA deletion analyses of the unmodified \"textbook\" E. coli core model: all single-gene deletions (call-50-19 -> single_gene_deletions.csv), all single-reaction deletions (call-96-9 -> single_reaction_deletions.csv), all unordered reaction-pair/single-reaction knockout sets (call-97-9 -> double_reaction_deletions.csv), plus the interpreted knockout demonstrations of the first section (calls 32-44 -> pfk_knockout_optima.csv). All four are requested outputs; no scientific branch of the source is silently dropped.\n\nINPUT DERIVATION. The recorded original-input manifest is empty because the source has no external data file: load_model(\"textbook\") reads cobrapy's bundled package data (cobra/data/textbook.xml.gz), confirmed offline-capable in outcome.json. The task input inputs/e_coli_core.xml is produced by gzip-decompressing that bundled file, so the solver receives the byte-exact SBML document the source parsed. No model attribute, medium, bound or objective is changed. The three recorded CSVs are copied byte-for-byte from the reference directory (their schema \u2014 knockouts,growth,status with labels formed by exports.py as sorted ';'-joined ids, empty growth for infeasible rows, unrounded floats including sub-1e-14 negative noise, statuses optimal/infeasible \u2014 already matches the public contract, so no re-serialization or projection is performed). Row counts 137 / 95 / 4560 (= 95 singletons + C(95,2) pairs, matching deletion.py's frozenset-population construction verified in the pinned review) are cross-checked against the reference structural observations.\n\nENDPOINT RECOVERY. The PFK/pfkA/pfkB optima existed only transiently inside with-blocks (printed, never stored; with-contexts restore the model). Per the endpoint-recovery policy, derive_code recovers them by rerunning the unchanged knockout/optimize sequence of source lines 32-44 on the same model: wild-type optimize(), PFK.knock_out() then optimize(), b1723 knock_out() then optimize(), then b3916 knock_out() (sequential, inside one with-block) then optimize(). Required state is only the freshly loaded model; lineage is fully documented here and the recovered file is written separately under destination/reference/pfk_knockout_optima.csv while the original reference artifacts are left untouched. This recovered endpoint still needs independent validation (it has no recorded baseline artifact; the private stdout cross-check 0.874/0.704/0.874/0.704 is consistent with the b1723 and PFK rows of recorded tables 1 and 2, but only the two gene-level rows b1723 and b1723;b3916 plus the wild type add information beyond those projections). The oracle computes the same four scenarios independently from the supplied model. Methods, inputs and populations are unchanged from the source.\n\nGRAIN AND ALIGNMENT. One row per knockout set (frozenset of gene or reaction ids), labels = ids sorted lexicographically and joined with ';' (exactly exports.py's convention; reference examples confirm e.g. 'Biomass_Ecoli_core;LDH_D'). Populations are every model gene (137) and every model reaction (95), including boundary/exchange reactions and genes with no reaction associations \u2014 no entity filtering or data loss. No duplicate-entity-key annotation issue arises (each row is a distinct knockout set). Infeasible rows carry solver status and empty growth, mirroring the recorded exports (2/2/352 empty growth cells).\n\nEXCLUSIONS (source-backed, distinguished from export-inventory limits). (1) The iJO1366 double-gene-deletion multiprocessing benchmark (call-26-14, calls 69-83) is a nondeterministic timing diagnostic framed solely as such by the narrative (\"Speedup of %.2fx\"); its deletion values are never consumed. The notebook's printed \"200 genes\" contradicting the 25-gene slice is a text bug in a diagnostic. (2) The positionally-sliced double_gene_deletion(cobra_model, cobra_model.genes[-5:]).round(4) (calls 64-65) is an API-mechanics demonstration whose value is discarded: it is a bare expression absent from the reference stdout, and .round(4) is display formatting; the narrative does not interpret its results. The review records this as a residual judgment call \u2014 faithful recomputation as a fifth output remains possible if validation disagrees; no source-faithful blocker exists. (3) The subset demonstrations single_gene_deletion(genes[:20]), single_reaction_deletion(reactions[:20]) and double_reaction_deletion(reactions[2:7]) are pure restrictions of retained tables 1-3 (classifiers flagged redundant against the producing whole-population calls). (4) The .knockout indexer prints are display reads of retained table rows.\n\nLEAKAGE. derive_code and oracle_code embed no measured answer values or reference-derived constants (gene/reaction ids PFK, b1723, b3916 and model filenames are input identifiers defined by the supplied model and the public question, not results). The oracle reads only inputs/e_coli_core.xml and uses installed packages; it never accesses destination/reference or any cache. The reference CSVs containing answers live only under destination/reference, which is hidden from the isolated oracle. Known environment consideration from the setup audit: cobrapy's package data necessarily contains the textbook model itself (an input, not an answer) and must be retained.\n\nREMAINING COMPARISON QUESTIONS (left to validation, not resolved here): replay observations show run-dependent row order (set iteration) and low-order float digit variation between LP solves, so comparison must be row-multiset based on the knockouts key with a numerical tolerance appropriate for LP-solver noise (including retaining tiny negative values and empty-vs-value infeasible rows rather than byte identity); and pfk_knockout_optima.csv has no recorded baseline and therefore needs independent scientific validation of its four values. Grading tolerances are deliberately not stated in the public question."

A separate worker receives the question and inputs without private reference or oracle access. Shared model families and dependency stacks limit independence and do not establish universal portability.

Prompt

autonomous-runs/226/explorer-evidence/grading/independent/system-prompt.md

Independently implement the public scientific task for validation

You receive only the public question, supplied task inputs, required output paths, installed environment and execution limits. You do not receive the reference answers or its solution code. This is a validation implementation, not the final blind benchmark attempt. It cannot establish universal software portability.

Use the offline shell to inspect inputs and develop a standalone Python program accepting --input-dir PATH and --output-dir PATH. Write only in your working directory and supplied output directory. Private answer/author directories are inaccessible; do not try to bypass those boundaries. Follow the public scientific requirements. Use the simplest compliant workflow with the installed tools allowed by the question, including domain libraries. Independence here means separately authored code without access to private answers or the reference program; it does not require a different software stack or reimplementation of library internals. Use basic numerical/statistical primitives when the task calls for them or the available library cannot express the required method. Check that a high-level method has the requested options and definitions rather than assuming equivalence from its name. Do not change the scientific method to obtain a convenient answer. Report ambiguity rather than guess hidden rules.

Choose a normal workflow allowed by the public question. If a requested saved artifact is also a natural hand-off to a later analysis step, use its saved representation at that boundary where feasible. Do not infer an in-memory-only requirement absent from the question. Avoid introducing gratuitously lossy formats or changing the scientific method for variation. Record the chosen boundary and its precision limitations in your rationale; do not claim that agreement with the hidden answer has been established.

Submit disposition: ready, the complete code, and a concise private rationale explaining methods and any limitations. The controller runs your program on the supplied inputs from a fresh output directory and returns execution failures for repair. It does not expose expected values or numerical grading feedback in this session. A later stage compares your outputs, examines scientific differences and validates acceptance rules. Do not claim agreement you have not observed.

Keep the implementation and inspection focused; submit a complete program rather than building your own grader or mutation suite. If blocked, return disposition: blocked, an empty code string and a specific explanation.

Use targeted development checks, then submit the complete program for the controller's fresh end-to-end execution on the unchanged supplied inputs. Do not repeatedly run the full analysis merely to check your own determinism, calibrate acceptance tolerances, or compare against a second reference program you wrote yourself. Those checks do not establish agreement with the hidden answer. Diagnose a concrete execution failure when it occurs; otherwise hand off the runnable program and its unresolved limitations. Cleaning exploratory files is not required for submission: the returned code is the artifact the controller executes. Do not delete useful diagnostic evidence just to tidy the workspace.

Repairing your earlier implementation

When repair is supplied, the earlier independently authored program did not establish the required comparison. You receive that program and exact paired quotes from the unchanged public question and your prior code. Inspect whether that code satisfies the quoted requirement, then repair your implementation using only the public question, original inputs and installed environment. The private diagnostic reasoning, reference program, grader and expected values are not supplied. Do not infer them or weaken the scientific requirement. Return a complete program for fresh execution. Preserve the original methods and input/output contract; report a blocker if those cannot be met. This is a repaired independent check, not a fresh blind benchmark attempt. No additional quality-repair campaign is available if the new comparison remains unresolved.

Shell execution

Keep diagnostics concise: print aggregate checks and representative examples. Save complete listings to scratch files and inspect selected sections instead of streaming all rows, arrays or mismatches into the conversation.

Run commands in the foreground. Each shell call terminates its remaining child processes when it returns; background/nohup work cannot continue between calls. For longer computations, explicitly set timeout_sec up to the supplied reference_seconds limit (the shell default is 120 seconds). Save useful results to files before returning, then inspect them in later calls.

  "public_instruction": "# Growth effects of gene and reaction knockouts in the E. coli core metabolic model\n\n## Objective\nYou are given the curated \"textbook\" E. coli core metabolic model (BiGG id `e_coli_core`) as an SBML file. Using flux balance analysis (FBA), determine how every possible single-gene deletion, every single-reaction deletion, every pairwise reaction deletion, and four specific knockout scenarios that illustrate gene-level redundancy for phosphofructokinase affect the maximal achievable growth.\n\nBy \"growth\" we mean the optimal value of the model's biomass objective (the raw LP objective value; no rounding, clamping or sign correction). For every knockout scenario, report that optimum together with the status reported by the LP solve (e.g. `optimal` or `infeasible`).\n\n## Supplied input\n- `inputs/e_coli_core.xml` \u2014 the E. coli core metabolic model in SBML format, including its biomass objective reaction and gene\u2013protein\u2013reaction (GPR) associations. Use the model exactly as supplied; do not modify it, its medium, bounds or objective.\n\n## Knockout semantics\n- **Reaction knockout**: the reaction carries no flux; its flux is constrained to zero in both directions.\n- **Gene knockout**: a reaction is disabled only if its GPR rule evaluates to false once the knocked-out gene(s) are removed. If a reaction has a remaining functional isozyme gene (an OR in the GPR), the reaction still carries flux; a gene whose removal disables no reaction therefore has no growth effect even though the gene is knocked out.\n\n## Required outputs\nProduce four CSV files, all with the columns `knockouts,growth,status`:\n\n- `knockouts`: the identifier(s) of the knocked-out entity, exactly as defined in the supplied model. For a knockout of multiple entities, the ids are sorted lexicographically and joined with `;` (e.g. `b1723;b3916`, `Biomass_Ecoli_core;LDH_D`); a single-entity knockout uses just that entity's id.\n- `growth`: the optimal objective value of the LP after the knockout, as reported by the solver at full double precision, with no rounding, clamping or sign correction. Tiny negative values of magnitude around 1e-14 that arise from solver noise are expected and must be reported as-is. Leave this field empty when the knockout makes the problem infeasible.\n- `status`: the LP solve status string, e.g. `optimal` or `infeasible`.\n\n### 1. `single_gene_deletions.csv`\nOne row for **every gene defined in the supplied model** (137 genes), including genes whose deletion disables no reaction.\n\n### 2. `single_reaction_deletions.csv`\nOne row for **every reaction defined in the supplied model** (95 reactions, including boundary/exchange reactions).\n\n### 3. `double_reaction_deletions.csv`\nOne row for **each distinct knockout set {r_i, r_j}** obtained by pairing every reaction in the model with every reaction in the model and reducing each ordered pair to an unordered set; the i = j cases contribute the single-reaction sets {r_i}. This yields the 95 singleton sets plus all C(95,2) = 4465 pairs, i.e. 4560 rows. Do not apply gene-level GPR logic here \u2014 both reactions are knocked out directly.\n\n### 4. `pfk_knockout_optima.csv`\nExactly four rows, with the same column convention and an empty `knockouts` field for the no-knockout row:\n\n- *(empty)* \u2014 the unmodified (wild-type) model, no knockout;\n- `PFK` \u2014 the PFK reaction knocked out;\n- `b1723` \u2014 gene b1723 (pfkA) knocked out;\n- `b1723;b3916` \u2014 genes b1723 (pfkA) and b3916 (pfkB) knocked out simultaneously.\n\nThese quantify isozyme redundancy: the isozyme pfkB can compensate for a pfkA deletion, but not when both genes are removed.\n\n## Conventions\n- Row order in every file carries no scientific meaning; any row ordering is acceptable.\n- Growth is reported in the model's native biomass-objective units (the raw LP objective value).\n- Use the knockout populations exactly as defined above; do not skip entities that have no reaction associations or no growth effect.\n- Do not round any value (`growth` is written at full double precision).\n\n## Environment and resources\nCPU only (up to 4 cores), 8 GiB RAM, no network access. Your program must complete within 600 seconds. Any software stack that satisfies the definitions above is acceptable; the results, not the tool, are what is compared.\n\nExact acceptance criteria (including numerical tolerances appropriate for LP-solver variation) are finalized separately during validation before the contract takes effect; produce results faithful to the definitions above.\n",
  "reference_seconds": 600
}

{
  "code": "#!/usr/bin/env python\n\"\"\"Growth effects of gene/reaction knockouts in the E. coli core model (FBA).\n\nInputs (read-only):\n    <input-dir>/e_coli_core.xml\n\nOutputs (in <output-dir>):\n    single_gene_deletions.csv\n    single_reaction_deletions.csv\n    double_reaction_deletions.csv\n    pfk_knockout_optima.csv\n\nAll files have columns: knockouts,growth,status\n - knockouts: entity ids, lexicographically sorted, ';'-joined\n - growth: raw LP objective value at full double precision (repr),\n   empty when the solve is not optimal\n - status: solver status string, e.g. 'optimal' or 'infeasible'\n\"\"\"\nimport argparse\nimport os\n\nimport cobra\nfrom cobra.flux_analysis import (\n    double_reaction_deletion,\n    single_gene_deletion,\n    single_reaction_deletion,\n)\nimport pandas as pd\n\n\ndef growth_str(growth, status):\n    \"\"\"Format the raw LP optimum, leaving it empty for non-optimal solves.\"\"\"\n    if status != \"optimal\" or pd.isna(growth):\n        return \"\"\n    return repr(float(growth))\n\n\ndef write_frame(df, path):\n    \"\"\"Convert a cobra deletion DataFrame ('ids','growth','status') to CSV.\"\"\"\n    rows = []\n    for _, r in df.iterrows():\n        ids = sorted(r[\"ids\"])  # frozenset of ids -> sorted list\n        rows.append({\n            \"knockouts\": \";\".join(ids),\n            \"growth\": growth_str(r[\"growth\"], r[\"status\"]),\n            \"status\": r[\"status\"],\n        })\n    out = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=[\"knockouts\", \"growth\", \"status\"])\n    out.to_csv(path, index=False)\n\n\ndef main():\n    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()\n    ap.add_argument(\"--input-dir\", required=True)\n    ap.add_argument(\"--output-dir\", required=True)\n    args = ap.parse_args()\n\n    os.makedirs(args.output_dir, exist_ok=True)\n\n    model = cobra.io.read_sbml_model(\n        os.path.join(args.input_dir, \"e_coli_core.xml\")\n    )\n\n    # 1. every single gene deletion (137 genes, incl. no-effect genes)\n    res = single_gene_deletion(model, processes=4)\n    write_frame(res, os.path.join(args.output_dir, \"single_gene_deletions.csv\"))\n\n    # 2. every single reaction deletion (95 reactions, incl. exchanges)\n    res = single_reaction_deletion(model, processes=4)\n    write_frame(res, os.path.join(args.output_dir, \"single_reaction_deletions.csv\"))\n\n    # 3. every distinct pair (plus singletons): 95 + C(95,2) = 4560 rows\n    res = double_reaction_deletion(model, processes=4)\n    write_frame(res, os.path.join(args.output_dir, \"double_reaction_deletions.csv\"))\n\n    # 4. PFK / pfkA / pfkB knockout scenarios\n    with model:\n        rows = []\n\n        # wild type (no knockout)\n        growth = model.slim_optimize()\n        rows.append((\"\", growth, model.solver.status))\n\n        # PFK reaction knockout\n        model.reactions.PFK.knock_out()\n        growth = model.slim_optimize()\n        rows.append((\"PFK\", growth, model.solver.status))\n\n        # restore, then gene b1723 (pfkA) knockout only\n    with model:\n        model.genes.b1723.knock_out()\n        growth = model.slim_optimize()\n        rows.append((\"b1723\", growth, model.solver.status))\n\n    with model:\n        # genes b1723 (pfkA) and b3916 (pfkB) knocked out simultaneously\n        model.genes.b1723.knock_out()\n        model.genes.b3916.knock_out()\n        growth = model.slim_optimize()\n        rows.append((\"b1723;b3916\", growth, model.solver.status))\n\n    rows_out = [\n        {\n            \"knockouts\": ko,\n            \"growth\": growth_str(g, st),\n            \"status\": st,\n        }\n        for (ko, g, st) in rows\n    ]\n    pd.DataFrame(rows_out, columns=[\"knockouts\", \"growth\", \"status\"]).to_csv(\n        os.path.join(args.output_dir, \"pfk_knockout_optima.csv\"), index=False\n    )\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    main()\n",
  "disposition": "ready",
  "rationale": "Uses cobra 0.32.1 (installed) with its native deletion machinery, which implements exactly the public knockout semantics: reaction KO via Reaction.knock_out() (flux forced to zero both directions) and gene KO via Gene.knock_out() (GPR evaluation, isozyme ORs preserved). Model file is loaded unmodified from --input-dir/e_coli_core.xml. single_gene_deletion and single_reaction_deletion cover all model-defined genes/reactants; double_reaction_deletion enumerates all 95+C(95,2)=4560 unordered sets exactly as specified (cobra reduces ordered pairs to frozensets). The four PFK rows are computed by direct model-controlled knockouts (wild type, PFK reaction, gene b1723, genes b1723+B3916) using slim_optimize, reporting the raw LP objective and model.solver.status with model state restored between contexts. growth is written at full double precision via repr (e.g. tiny negatives like -3.64e-15 kept as-is) and is left empty with status 'infeasible' when the LP is infeasible. Boundary choice: cobra's DataFrame (ids/growth/status) is the saved/artifact boundary; ids are sorted lexicographically and ';'-joined, except the m**a prior version's stray line was removed and PFK rows are computed on fresh model contexts. Verified end-to-end on supplied input: 137/95/4560/4 rows, statuses optimal/infeasible consistent with FBA expectations. No confirmation of agreement with the hidden reference has been established - only that outputs match the stated public contract. Runtime ~35 s including a full double-deletion run, well under the 600 s limit."

    "code": "#!/usr/bin/env python\n\"\"\"Growth effects of gene/reaction knockouts in the E. coli core model (FBA).\n\nInputs (read-only):\n    <input-dir>/e_coli_core.xml\n\nOutputs (in <output-dir>):\n    single_gene_deletions.csv\n    single_reaction_deletions.csv\n    double_reaction_deletions.csv\n    pfk_knockout_optima.csv\n\nAll files have columns: knockouts,growth,status\n - knockouts: entity ids, lexicographically sorted, ';'-joined\n - growth: raw LP objective value at full double precision (repr),\n   empty when the solve is not optimal\n - status: solver status string, e.g. 'optimal' or 'infeasible'\n\"\"\"\nimport argparse\nimport os\n\nimport cobra\nfrom cobra.flux_analysis import (\n    double_reaction_deletion,\n    single_gene_deletion,\n    single_reaction_deletion,\n)\nimport pandas as pd\n\n\ndef growth_str(growth, status):\n    \"\"\"Format the raw LP optimum, leaving it empty for non-optimal solves.\"\"\"\n    if status != \"optimal\" or pd.isna(growth):\n        return \"\"\n    return repr(float(growth))\n\n\ndef write_frame(df, path):\n    \"\"\"Convert a cobra deletion DataFrame ('ids','growth','status') to CSV.\"\"\"\n    rows = []\n    for _, r in df.iterrows():\n        ids = sorted(r[\"ids\"])  # frozenset of ids -> sorted list\n        rows.append({\n            \"knockouts\": \";\".join(ids),\n            \"growth\": growth_str(r[\"growth\"], r[\"status\"]),\n            \"status\": r[\"status\"],\n        })\n    out = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=[\"knockouts\", \"growth\", \"status\"])\n    out.to_csv(path, index=False)\n\n\ndef main():\n    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()\n    ap.add_argument(\"--input-dir\", required=True)\n    ap.add_argument(\"--output-dir\", required=True)\n    args = ap.parse_args()\n\n    os.makedirs(args.output_dir, exist_ok=True)\n\n    model = cobra.io.read_sbml_model(\n        os.path.join(args.input_dir, \"e_coli_core.xml\")\n    )\n\n    # 1. every single gene deletion (137 genes, incl. no-effect genes)\n    res = single_gene_deletion(model, processes=4)\n    write_frame(res, os.path.join(args.output_dir, \"single_gene_deletions.csv\"))\n\n    # 2. every single reaction deletion (95 reactions, incl. exchanges)\n    res = single_reaction_deletion(model, processes=4)\n    write_frame(res, os.path.join(args.output_dir, \"single_reaction_deletions.csv\"))\n\n    # 3. every distinct pair (plus singletons): 95 + C(95,2) = 4560 rows\n    res = double_reaction_deletion(model, processes=4)\n    write_frame(res, os.path.join(args.output_dir, \"double_reaction_deletions.csv\"))\n\n    # 4. PFK / pfkA / pfkB knockout scenarios\n    with model:\n        rows = []\n\n        # wild type (no knockout)\n        growth = model.slim_optimize()\n        rows.append((\"\", growth, model.solver.status))\n\n        # PFK reaction knockout\n        model.reactions.PFK.knock_out()\n        growth = model.slim_optimize()\n        rows.append((\"PFK\", growth, model.solver.status))\n\n        # restore, then gene b1723 (pfkA) knockout only\n    with model:\n        model.genes.b1723.knock_out()\n        growth = model.slim_optimize()\n        rows.append((\"b1723\", growth, model.solver.status))\n\n    with model:\n        # genes b1723 (pfkA) and b3916 (pfkB) knocked out simultaneously\n        model.genes.b1723.knock_out()\n        model.genes.b3916.knock_out()\n        growth = model.slim_optimize()\n        rows.append((\"b1723;b3916\", growth, model.solver.status))\n\n    rows_out = [\n        {\n            \"knockouts\": ko,\n            \"growth\": growth_str(g, st),\n            \"status\": st,\n        }\n        for (ko, g, st) in rows\n    ]\n    pd.DataFrame(rows_out, columns=[\"knockouts\", \"growth\", \"status\"]).to_csv(\n        os.path.join(args.output_dir, \"pfk_knockout_optima.csv\"), index=False\n    )\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    main()\n",
    "disposition": "ready",
    "rationale": "Uses cobra 0.32.1 (installed) with its native deletion machinery, which implements exactly the public knockout semantics: reaction KO via Reaction.knock_out() (flux forced to zero both directions) and gene KO via Gene.knock_out() (GPR evaluation, isozyme ORs preserved). Model file is loaded unmodified from --input-dir/e_coli_core.xml. single_gene_deletion and single_reaction_deletion cover all model-defined genes/reactants; double_reaction_deletion enumerates all 95+C(95,2)=4560 unordered sets exactly as specified (cobra reduces ordered pairs to frozensets). The four PFK rows are computed by direct model-controlled knockouts (wild type, PFK reaction, gene b1723, genes b1723+B3916) using slim_optimize, reporting the raw LP objective and model.solver.status with model state restored between contexts. growth is written at full double precision via repr (e.g. tiny negatives like -3.64e-15 kept as-is) and is left empty with status 'infeasible' when the LP is infeasible. Boundary choice: cobra's DataFrame (ids/growth/status) is the saved/artifact boundary; ids are sorted lexicographically and ';'-joined, except the m**a prior version's stray line was removed and PFK rows are computed on fresh model contexts. Verified end-to-end on supplied input: 137/95/4560/4 rows, statuses optimal/infeasible consistent with FBA expectations. No confirmation of agreement with the hidden reference has been established - only that outputs match the stated public contract. Runtime ~35 s including a full double-deletion run, well under the 600 s limit."

      "instruction": "# Growth effects of gene and reaction knockouts in the E. coli core metabolic model\n\n## Objective\nYou are given the curated \"textbook\" E. coli core metabolic model (BiGG id `e_coli_core`) as an SBML file. Using flux balance analysis (FBA), determine how every possible single-gene deletion, every single-reaction deletion, every pairwise reaction deletion, and four specific knockout scenarios that illustrate gene-level redundancy for phosphofructokinase affect the maximal achievable growth.\n\nBy \"growth\" we mean the optimal value of the model's biomass objective (the raw LP objective value; no rounding, clamping or sign correction). For every knockout scenario, report that optimum together with the status reported by the LP solve (e.g. `optimal` or `infeasible`).\n\n## Supplied input\n- `inputs/e_coli_core.xml` \u2014 the E. coli core metabolic model in SBML format, including its biomass objective reaction and gene\u2013protein\u2013reaction (GPR) associations. Use the model exactly as supplied; do not modify it, its medium, bounds or objective.\n\n## Knockout semantics\n- **Reaction knockout**: the reaction carries no flux; its flux is constrained to zero in both directions.\n- **Gene knockout**: a reaction is disabled only if its GPR rule evaluates to false once the knocked-out gene(s) are removed. If a reaction has a remaining functional isozyme gene (an OR in the GPR), the reaction still carries flux; a gene whose removal disables no reaction therefore has no growth effect even though the gene is knocked out.\n\n## Required outputs\nProduce four CSV files, all with the columns `knockouts,growth,status`:\n\n- `knockouts`: the identifier(s) of the knocked-out entity, exactly as defined in the supplied model. For a knockout of multiple entities, the ids are sorted lexicographically and joined with `;` (e.g. `b1723;b3916`, `Biomass_Ecoli_core;LDH_D`); a single-entity knockout uses just that entity's id.\n- `growth`: the optimal objective value of the LP after the knockout, as reported by the solver at full double precision, with no rounding, clamping or sign correction. Tiny negative values of magnitude around 1e-14 that arise from solver noise are expected and must be reported as-is. Leave this field empty when the knockout makes the problem infeasible.\n- `status`: the LP solve status string, e.g. `optimal` or `infeasible`.\n\n### 1. `single_gene_deletions.csv`\nOne row for **every gene defined in the supplied model** (137 genes), including genes whose deletion disables no reaction.\n\n### 2. `single_reaction_deletions.csv`\nOne row for **every reaction defined in the supplied model** (95 reactions, including boundary/exchange reactions).\n\n### 3. `double_reaction_deletions.csv`\nOne row for **each distinct knockout set {r_i, r_j}** obtained by pairing every reaction in the model with every reaction in the model and reducing each ordered pair to an unordered set; the i = j cases contribute the single-reaction sets {r_i}. This yields the 95 singleton sets plus all C(95,2) = 4465 pairs, i.e. 4560 rows. Do not apply gene-level GPR logic here \u2014 both reactions are knocked out directly.\n\n### 4. `pfk_knockout_optima.csv`\nExactly four rows, with the same column convention and an empty `knockouts` field for the no-knockout row:\n\n- *(empty)* \u2014 the unmodified (wild-type) model, no knockout;\n- `PFK` \u2014 the PFK reaction knocked out;\n- `b1723` \u2014 gene b1723 (pfkA) knocked out;\n- `b1723;b3916` \u2014 genes b1723 (pfkA) and b3916 (pfkB) knocked out simultaneously.\n\nThese quantify isozyme redundancy: the isozyme pfkB can compensate for a pfkA deletion, but not when both genes are removed.\n\n## Conventions\n- Row order in every file carries no scientific meaning; any row ordering is acceptable.\n- Growth is reported in the model's native biomass-objective units (the raw LP objective value).\n- Use the knockout populations exactly as defined above; do not skip entities that have no reaction associations or no growth effect.\n- Do not round any value (`growth` is written at full double precision).\n\n## Environment and resources\nCPU only (up to 4 cores), 8 GiB RAM, no network access. Your program must complete within 600 seconds. Any software stack that satisfies the definitions above is acceptable; the results, not the tool, are what is compared.\n\nExact acceptance criteria (including numerical tolerances appropriate for LP-solver variation) are finalized separately during validation before the contract takes effect; produce results faithful to the definitions above.\n",

return \"\"\n    return repr(value)\n\n\ndef _format_knockouts(ids):\n    return \";\".join(sorted(str(identifier) for identifier in ids))\n\n\ndef _frame_rows(frame):\n    if \"ids\" in parser.add_argument(\"--input-dir\", required=True)\n    parser.add_argument(\"--output-dir\", required=True)\n    args = parser.parse_args()\n\n    from cobra.io import read_sbml_model\n    from cobra.flux_analysis import (\n        single_gene_deletion,\n        single_reaction_deletion,\n        double_reaction_deletion,\n    )\n\n    model = read_sbml_model(os.path.join(args.input_dir, \"e_coli_core.xml\"))\n    os.makedirs(args.output_dir, exist_ok=True)\n\n    gene_frame = single_gene_deletion(model)\n    reaction_frame = single_reaction_deletion(model)\n    double_frame = double_reaction_deletion(model)\n\n    header = \"knockouts,growth,status\"\n    _write_csv(\n        os.path.join(args.output_dir, \"single_gene_deletions.csv\"),\n        header,\n model.reactions.PFK.knock_out()\n        solution = model.optimize()\n        rows.append((\"PFK\", _format_growth(solution.objective_value), solution.status))\n    with model:\n
